nights.themeLine: Prices, pencils and empires: how big systems run (or fall) without a centre. Then an AI that could spread with no off switch.
nights.learn: Why prices work like a giant information network that no central planner could ever replace.

paper.title: The Use of Knowledge in Society

ai.title: AI Models May Be Capable of Self-Replicating Without Access to a Datacenter
ai.note: Small AI models may soon be able to copy themselves onto cheap gadgets like TV boxes, with no datacenter needed.

story.title: How Much Land Does a Man Need?
story.note: A peasant who can't stop wanting more.

essay.title: I, Pencil
essay.note: Hayek's idea told by a pencil: no one person knows how to make one.

nights.themeLine: Gettier asks when a true belief counts as knowledge. Chekhov's reader, Stevens's thirteen viewpoints and Epictetus test what we can be sure of. Nadella asks whether we can trust our AI at all.
nights.learn: Why "a true belief with good reasons" isn't the same as knowing something. Three pages that upset a definition going back to Plato.

ai.title: Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era
ai.note: Microsoft's boss argues companies should treat AI models like a possibly compromised employee, with an emergency brake outside the model.

story.title: The Bet
story.note: A lawyer bets 15 years of his life on reading.

poem.title: Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird

essay.title: The Enchiridion (first half)
essay.note: A Stoic's handbook: what is and isn't in your control.

nights.themeLine: A fly's brain mapped cell by cell, a mechanical being dissecting its own mind, and Acemoglu on what AI might do to the knowledge we share.
nights.learn: How scientists mapped every cell and connection in a fruit fly's brain (about 140,000 neurons) and what the map already reveals.

paper.title: Neuronal Wiring Diagram of an Adult Brain

ai.title: AI, Human Cognition and Knowledge Collapse
ai.note: A Nobel-winning economist's warning: AI that gives us great personal advice may slowly erode what we know collectively. Free PDF on the page.

story.title: Exhalation
story.note: Modern. A mechanical being opens up its own brain to see how it thinks.

essay.title: Cargo Cult Science
essay.note: How to tell real science from things that only look like it.

nights.themeLine: Miner, Montaigne and Bishop each make familiar people look foreign. Jemisin tours a perfect society, and AI agents struggle to understand their own humans.
nights.learn: How anthropologists make the familiar look strange. A famous satire that studies a "tribe" with odd body rituals (spell its name backwards).

ai.title: Project Swap: What Happens When Agents Trade for Us?
ai.note: 201 people's AI agents ran a book-swap market. The trading went well; knowing what their owners wanted didn't.

story.title: The Ones Who Stay and Fight
story.note: Modern. A guided tour of a near-perfect city, and what it costs.

poem.title: In the Waiting Room
poem.note: A seven-year-old, a National Geographic, and the shock of being one person among many.

essay.title: Of Cannibals
essay.note: "Everyone calls barbarous what is not his own custom." Written in 1580.

nights.theme: What we do with our time
nights.themeLine: A vaccine that may protect memory, one hour of unexpected freedom, Seneca on time as our only true possession, and AI's rapidly growing attention span.
nights.learn: How a birthday cut-off in Wales's vaccine rules created a natural experiment suggesting the shingles vaccine lowers dementia risk by about a fifth.

paper.title: A Natural Experiment on the Effect of Herpes Zoster Vaccination on Dementia

ai.title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks
ai.note: The chart everyone in AI cites: the length of tasks AI can do on its own keeps doubling.

essay.title: On Saving Time (Letter 1)
essay.note: At the top of the page.

nights.themeLine: Shklovsky says art exists to make the familiar strange again. Joyce, Collins and Orwell each do it with words, and Mollick argues for deciding on purpose when to let AI think for you.
nights.learn: "Defamiliarisation": the idea that art exists to make familiar things feel new again. It's the whole point of Bradbury's challenge.

ai.title: Choosing to Stay Human
ai.note: Why to decide on purpose when AI thinks for you, before "cognitive surrender" dulls your own judgment.

nights.themeLine: Purcell's bacteria live by different rules, chalk holds Earth's history in tiny shells, and an AI completes a calculation physicists thought was out of reach.
nights.learn: Why swimming is completely different for a bacterium. At its size water feels like thick syrup, and the usual tricks don't work.

paper.title: Life at Low Reynolds Number
paper.note: A Nobel-winning physicist's famously funny lecture.

ai.title: Yes, Claude Can Do Nine Loops
ai.note: A physicist dared AI labs to do a famously hard calculation on a small budget. Claude did it. Pairs with tonight's physics.

poem.title: When I Heard the Learn'd Astronomer

essay.title: On a Piece of Chalk
essay.note: What a lump of chalk reveals about Earth's history.

nights.themeLine: An AI restores missing letters on ancient stones, another fills in the unseen third of the sky, and Woolf asks how much of the Greeks we can ever recover.
nights.learn: How an AI called Ithaca fills in missing letters on worn ancient Greek inscriptions and guesses when and where they were carved, and how much it helps real historians.

paper.title: Restoring and Attributing Ancient Texts Using Deep Neural Networks

ai.title: The Missing Map of the Sky
ai.note: An astrophysicist used AI to build the first complete ultraviolet map of the sky, filling in the third nobody had observed.

nights.themeLine: Gale and Shapley's matching maths, O. Henry's doomed gifts, Shakespeare's "marriage of true minds", and new data on how AI is changing who gets hired.
nights.learn: The simple method for pairing people up so no two would rather swap. It now runs New York City's high school admissions and medical residency matching, and led to a Nobel Prize.

paper.title: College Admissions and the Stability of Marriage

ai.title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of AI
ai.note: No mass job losses yet, but young workers in AI-exposed jobs are 19% behind where they'd otherwise be.

poem.title: Sonnet 116
poem.note: "Let me not to the marriage of true minds…"

nights.themeLine: New brain research says language is for talking, not thinking. Inside Claude, thoughts seem to live beneath any one language. Paul Graham argues writing is thinking.
nights.learn: The evidence that we don't need language to think: people who lose their language can still reason, do maths and play chess.

paper.title: Language Is Primarily a Tool for Communication Rather than Thought

ai.title: Tracing the Thoughts of a Large Language Model
ai.note: Looking inside Claude, researchers found it often thinks in concepts shared across languages, not in English or French.

story.title: Mono no Aware
story.note: Modern. A story built around a single Japanese phrase.

essay.title: Writes and Write-Nots
essay.note: Argues the opposite: writing is thinking. A good fight with tonight's paper.
